proofs.proof_tex:
Put \(L=L_m\) and \(a=a_m\).  We first prove the finite Ferrers transport fact used throughout.  Let \((\rho_b)_{b=0}^H\) and \((\sigma_w)_{w=0}^H\) be nonnegative arrays with the same total mass.  A nonnegative array with these margins and support \(b+w\le H\) can exist only if
\[
 \sum_{b=h}^H\rho_b\le \sum_{w=0}^{H-h}\sigma_w,
 \qquad h=0,\ldots,H.                                      \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, every row in the left-hand tail has its neighborhood inside the column prefix on the right.  Conversely, process rows \(b=H,H-1,\ldots,0\), filling row \(b\) from the remaining mass in columns \(0,\ldots,H-b\).  Immediately before row \(b\) is filled, the previously processed rows have consumed exactly \(\sum_{r>b}\rho_r\) units from that prefix.  Its remaining mass is therefore
\[
 \sum_{w=0}^{H-b}\sigma_w-\sum_{r>b}\rho_r\ge \rho_b       \tag{2}
\]
by (1), so row \(b\) can be filled, splitting a column if necessary.  After the last row, equality of total masses forces every column residual to be zero.  Thus (1) is also sufficient, constructively, without strict Hall slack or positive cell masses.  This is the nested-neighborhood specialization of the Hall transport criterion, derived here by the descending-row algorithm.

Apply necessity to any member of \(\Gamma_H(p,q)\).  With \(h=H-s\), it gives
\[
 A_s=\sum_{b=H-s}^Hp_b\le Q_s=\sum_{w=0}^sq_w,
 \qquad s=0,\ldots,H.                                      \tag{3}
\]
Fix \(x\in\Gamma_H(p,q)\), define \(z_w=\sum_{b\ge m}x_{bw}\), and write \(Z_s=\sum_{w=0}^sz_w\).  If \(b\ge m\) and \(x_{bw}>0\), then \(w\le H-b\le H-m=L\).  Hence \(z_w=0\) for \(w>L\).  Nonnegativity and the column equations give \(0\le z_w\le q_w\), while the selected row equations give
\[
 Z_L=\sum_{b=m}^H\sum_wx_{bw}=\sum_{b=m}^Hp_b=a.            \tag{4}
\]
For \(0\le s\le L\), every row \(b\ge H-s\) is selected and can use only columns \(w\le s\), whence
\[
 Z_s\ge \sum_{b=H-s}^Hp_b=A_s.                             \tag{5}
\]

These conditions are sufficient.  Suppose \(z\) satisfies them.  Give rows \(b\ge m\) masses \(p_b\), rows \(b<m\) mass zero, and columns masses \(z_w\).  For \(h\ge m\), condition (1) is
\[
 \sum_{b=h}^Hp_b=A_{H-h}\le Z_{H-h};                       \tag{6}
\]
for \(h<m\), its left side is \(a\) and its right side is \(Z_L=a\).  The constructive sufficiency argument therefore produces a selected-row transport.  For the complementary rows, use row masses \(p_b\mathbf 1\{b<m\}\) and column masses \(q_w-z_w\).  The Hall inequalities are automatic for \(h\ge m\).  If \(h<m\), then \(H-h\ge L+1\), and the support and total-mass conditions on \(z\), followed by (3), give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \sum_{b=h}^{m-1}p_b
 &=\sum_{b=h}^Hp_b-a\\
 &\le Q_{H-h}-a
 =\sum_{w=0}^{H-h}(q_w-z_w).
 \end{aligned}                                             \tag{7}
\]
Thus the same algorithm produces the complementary transport.  Adding the two arrays gives an element of \(\Gamma_H(p,q)\) inducing exactly \(z\).  This proves the asserted characterization.

Every feasible cumulative array obeys \(Z_s\le a\) and \(Z_s\le Q_s\), hence
\[
 Z_s\le \min\{a,Q_s\}=Z_{ms}^{-}.                        \tag{8}
\]
The array \(Z_{ms}^{-}\) is feasible: (3) and \(A_s\le a\) give \(A_s\le Z_{ms}^{-}\); the increments of \(\min\{a,Q_s\}\) are nonnegative and no larger than the increments \(q_s\) of \(Q_s\); and (3) at \(s=L\) gives \(Q_L\ge A_L=a\), so \(Z_{mL}^{-}=a\).  The preceding characterization therefore makes \(Z_m^{-}\) attainable, and (8) makes it the pointwise maximal attainable cumulative array.  This argument also covers \(a=0\).

For the opposite extremum, feasibility implies, whenever \(s\le u\le L\),
\[
 Z_u-Z_s=\sum_{w=s+1}^uz_w\le Q_u-Q_s
 \quad\text{and}\quad Z_u\ge A_u.
\]
Consequently
\[
 Z_s\ge Q_s+A_u-Q_u,
 \qquad
 Z_s\ge Q_s+\max_{u=s,\ldots,L}(A_u-Q_u)=Z_{ms}^{+}.       \tag{9}
\]
Because \(A_L=a\), the terminal value is
\[
 Z_{mL}^{+}=Q_L+A_L-Q_L=a.                                \tag{10}
\]
Separating the term \(u=s\) from the maximum and using \(Q_{s+1}=Q_s+q_{s+1}\) yields the backward-deficit recursion
\[
 Z_{ms}^{+}=\max\{A_s,Z_{m,s+1}^{+}-q_{s+1}\},
 \qquad s<L.                                               \tag{11}
\]
Now \(A_s\le A_{s+1}\le Z_{m,s+1}^{+}\), so (11) gives \(Z_{ms}^{+}\le Z_{m,s+1}^{+}\) and \(Z_{m,s+1}^{+}-Z_{ms}^{+}\le q_{s+1}\).  At \(s=0\), the term \(u=0\) in the maximum gives \(Z_{m0}^{+}\ge A_0\ge0\), whereas (3) gives \(A_u-Q_u\le0\) for every \(u\), and hence \(Z_{m0}^{+}\le Q_0=q_0\).  Thus every increment of \(Z_m^{+}\) lies in \([0,q_w]\); (10) gives total mass \(a\); and (11) gives \(Z_{ms}^{+}\ge A_s\).  The characterization already proved makes this array attainable.  Inequality (9) makes it the pointwise minimal attainable cumulative array.

For any subdistribution supported on \(0,\ldots,L\) with total mass \(a\), finite summation by parts gives
\[
 \sum_{w=0}^{L}wz_w
 =\sum_{s=0}^{L-1}\sum_{w=s+1}^{L}z_w
 =La-\sum_{s=0}^{L-1}Z_s.                                 \tag{12}
\]
The maximal cumulative array \(Z_m^{-}\) therefore minimizes (12), and the minimal cumulative array \(Z_m^{+}\) maximizes it.  Both extrema are attained by the transports constructed above.

Finally, the fixed \((B,T)\) margin and \(\mu_b=\sum_ttp_{bt}\) give, for every compatible plan,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 J_m
 &=\pi\,\mathsf E[T\mathbf 1\{B<m\}+W\mathbf 1\{B\ge m\}\mid S_k^1=1]\\
 &=\pi\left(\sum_{b<m}\mu_b+\sum_{b\ge m,w}wx_{bw}\right).               \tag{13}
 \end{aligned}
\]
Every attaining \(x\) extends to a triple coupling by \(\text{lem:triple-projection-and-extension}\), including zero rows because no division is then performed, and \(\text{thm:causal-response-tree-lift}\) realizes that triple by a raw-path law with the same observed pushforward.  Therefore (12)--(13) give the stated sharp causal endpoints, not merely outer algebraic bounds.  All arguments remain valid at Hall equalities.

Fix an observable law \(P_O\) admitted by the maintained model, and let \(p_{bt}\), \(q_w\), and \(\pi>0\) be its identified margins.  Distinguish the causal identified set from its proposed observed-law representation by defining
\[
 \Theta_I(P_O)=\left\{(J_m(\widetilde{\mathsf P}))_{m\in\mathcal M}:
 \widetilde{\mathsf P}\in\mathfrak M_H,
 \ \widetilde{\mathsf P}_O=P_O\right\}.                  \tag{1}
\]
For any compatible law, the converse in \(\text{thm:causal-response-tree-lift}\) supplies \(\gamma\in\mathcal G_H(p_{BT},q)\).  Its projection \(x_{bw}=\sum_t\gamma_{btw}\) belongs to \(\Gamma_H(p,q)\) by \(\text{lem:triple-projection-and-extension}\).  Since the \((B,T)\) margin is fixed,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 J_m
 &=\pi\,\mathsf E[T\mathbf 1\{B<m\}+W\mathbf 1\{B\ge m\}\mid S_k^1=1]\\
 &=\pi\left(\sum_{b<m}\sum_ttp_{bt}+\sum_{b\ge m,w}wx_{bw}\right)\\
 &=\pi\left(\sum_{b<m}\mu_b+\sum_{b\ge m,w}wx_{bw}\right).              \tag{2}
 \end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(\Theta_I(P_O)\subseteq\mathcal V(p_{BT},q)\).  Conversely, for every \(x\in\Gamma_H(p,q)\), the extension part of \(\text{lem:triple-projection-and-extension}\) produces \(\gamma\in\mathcal G_H(p_{BT},q)\), and the forward part of \(\text{thm:causal-response-tree-lift}\) realizes that triple under a law with observed pushforward \(P_O\).  Equation (2) gives the associated point of \(\mathcal V(p_{BT},q)\).  Hence
\[
 \Theta_I(P_O)=\mathcal V(p_{BT},q).                       \tag{3}
\]
This proves joint sharpness.  Since \(\Gamma_H(p,q)\) is a nonempty compact convex polytope and (2) is affine in \(x\), the identified set is compact and convex.

For any \(\lambda\in\mathbb R^{|\mathcal M|}\), finite-sum rearrangement gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \lambda^\top J(x)
 &=\pi\sum_{m\in\mathcal M}\lambda_m\sum_{b<m}\mu_b
   +\pi\sum_{b,w}wx_{bw}\sum_{m\in\mathcal M}\lambda_m\mathbf 1\{b\ge m\}\\
 &=\pi\left[\sum_{m\in\mathcal M}\lambda_m\sum_{b<m}\mu_b
   +\sum_{b,w}c_b(\lambda)wx_{bw}\right].                 \tag{4}
 \end{aligned}
\]
Taking the maximum over \(x\in\Gamma_H(p,q)\), which is attained by compactness, is exactly \(h_{\mathcal V}(\lambda)\) in \(\text{def:support-function}\).

Write \(v_b(x)=\sum_wwx_{bw}\).  If \(m<j\), cancellation outside rows \(m,\ldots,j-1\) in (2) gives
\[
 J_m(x)-J_j(x)=\pi\sum_{b=m}^{j-1}\{v_b(x)-\mu_b\}.       \tag{5}
\]
Maximizing (5) yields
\[
 D_{mj}=\pi\left[\max_{x\in\Gamma_H(p,q)}
 \sum_{b=m}^{j-1}\sum_wwx_{bw}-\sum_{b=m}^{j-1}\mu_b\right].              \tag{6}
\]
If \(m>j\), the same cancellation gives
\[
 J_m(x)-J_j(x)=\pi\sum_{b=j}^{m-1}\{\mu_b-v_b(x)\},       \tag{7}
\]
and maximizing (7) gives the stated formula with the transport minimum; \(D_{mm}=0\).  Off-diagonal signs are unrestricted.  For a concrete negative value, take \(H=2\), \(p_1=1\), \(q_0=1\), \(p_{1,1}=1\), \(\pi=1\), and \(\mathcal M=\{1,2\}\).  The unique capacity-feasible residual is \(W=0\), so \(J_1=0\), \(J_2=1\), and \(D_{12}=-1\).

For a fixed deterministic threshold \(m\), its shared-law worst-case regret is
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \sup_{v\in\mathcal V}\left\{v_m-\min_{j\in\mathcal M}v_j\right\}
 &=\sup_{v\in\mathcal V}\max_{j\in\mathcal M}(v_m-v_j)\\
 &=\max_{j\in\mathcal M}\sup_{v\in\mathcal V}(v_m-v_j)
 =\max_{j\in\mathcal M}D_{mj}=R_m.                       \tag{8}
 \end{aligned}
\]
The interchange is exact because \(\mathcal M\) is finite: both sides are the supremum over \(\mathcal V\times\mathcal M\).  The comparator \(j=m\) gives \(R_m\ge0\).  Minimization over the nonempty finite menu therefore yields precisely \(\mathcal M^\star=\operatorname*{argmin}_{m\in\mathcal M}R_m\), retaining every tie.

Coordinate projection always gives
\[
 \mathcal V(p_{BT},q)\subseteq
 \prod_{m\in\mathcal M}[\underline J_m,\overline J_m].    \tag{9}
\]
It can be strict.  Take \(H=3\), \(p=(2/5,3/10,1/5,1/10)\), \(q=(3/10,3/10,1/5,1/5)\), \(\pi=1\), \(\mu=(0,7/20,7/40,0)\), and \(\mathcal M=\{1,2,3\}\).  The plan with nonzero cells
\[
 x_{00}=1/5,\quad x_{03}=1/5,\quad x_{11}=1/10,\quad
 x_{12}=1/5,\quad x_{21}=1/5,\quad x_{30}=1/10             \tag{10}
\]
is feasible and gives \(J_1=7/10\).  This is the upper endpoint: the total column first moment is \(13/10\), while row zero has mass \(2/5\) and must absorb the column-three mass \(1/5\), so its first moment is at least \(3/5\), leaving at most \(7/10\) for selected rows.  The plan with nonzero cells
\[
 x_{02}=1/5,\quad x_{03}=1/5,\quad x_{11}=3/10,\quad
 x_{20}=1/5,\quad x_{30}=1/10                              \tag{11}
\]
is feasible and gives \(J_2=7/20\), the lower endpoint because its residual contribution is nonnegative.  If one plan generated both coordinate extrema, (2) would imply \(v_2=0\) and \(v_1+v_2=7/10\), hence \(v_1=7/10\).  But row \(b=1\) has mass \(3/10\) and capacity ceiling \(w=2\), so \(v_1\le3/5<7/10\), a contradiction.  Thus (9) is in general a strict outer rectangle rather than the joint identified set.

All calculations use exact rational arithmetic.  The nontrivial Hall tail-prefix comparisons are
\[
 \begin{array}{c|ccc}
 h&1&2&3\\ \hline
 \sum_{b\ge h}p_b&3/5&3/10&1/10\\
 \sum_{w\le3-h}q_w&4/5&3/5&3/10
 \end{array}                                                \tag{1}
\]
and hence \(\Gamma_3(p,q)\ne\varnothing\).

For \(m=1\), \(L_1=2\), \(a_1=3/5\), and
\[
 (A_0,A_1,A_2)=(1/10,3/10,3/5),\qquad
 (Q_0,Q_1,Q_2)=(3/10,3/5,4/5).
\]
Therefore
\[
 (Z_{1s}^{-})_{s=0}^2=(3/10,3/5,3/5),\qquad
 (Z_{1s}^{+})_{s=0}^2=(1/10,2/5,3/5).                     \tag{2}
\]
The sharp endpoint formula and \(\mu_0=0\) give
\[
 J_1\in\left[2(3/5)-(3/10+3/5),
               2(3/5)-(1/10+2/5)\right]=[3/10,7/10].     \tag{3}
\]
For \(m=2\), \(L_2=1\), \(a_2=3/10\),
\[
 (A_0,A_1)=(1/10,3/10),\qquad (Q_0,Q_1)=(3/10,3/5),
\]
so \(Z_{20}^{-}=3/10\) and \(Z_{20}^{+}=1/10\).  Since \(\sum_{b<2}\mu_b=7/20\),
\[
 J_2\in[7/20,7/20+1/5]=[7/20,11/20].                     \tag{4}
\]
For \(m=3\), capacity forces row three into column zero, and therefore
\[
 J_3=\mu_0+\mu_1+\mu_2=21/40.                            \tag{5}
\]

For the pairwise calculations, the eligibility-greedy support theorem, applied to row-shell indicator coefficients and their negatives, gives
\[
 \begin{array}{c|cc}
 E&\min_{x\in\Gamma_3}\sum_{b\in E,w}wx_{bw}
   &\max_{x\in\Gamma_3}\sum_{b\in E,w}wx_{bw}\\ \hline
 \{1\}&1/10&1/2\\
 \{2\}&0&1/5\\
 \{1,2\}&3/10&7/10.
 \end{array}                                                \tag{6}
\]
These values have direct capacity certificates.  Row three consumes \(1/10\) of column zero, leaving at most \(1/5\) of that column for row one; its remaining \(1/10\) mass must have \(w\ge1\), so its first moment is at least \(1/10\).  For the row-one maximum, only \(1/5\) mass exists in column two and its remaining \(1/10\) mass has \(w\le1\), giving at most \(1/2\).  Row two has mass \(1/5\) and ceiling one, giving the bounds zero and \(1/5\).  For rows one and two together, row zero must absorb column-three mass \(1/5\), so subtracting its first moment from the total column first moment \(13/10\) gives an upper bound \(7/10\); conversely row zero has mass \(2/5\) and can absorb at most columns three and two, with first moment one, giving the lower bound \(13/10-1=3/10\).  The following feasible allocations attain the six respective extremes: for row one, use \((x_{10},x_{11})=(1/5,1/10)\) for the minimum and \((x_{11},x_{12})=(1/10,1/5)\) for the maximum; for row two, use \(x_{20}=1/5\) and \(x_{21}=1/5\); for the combined shell, use \((x_{11},x_{20},x_{30})=(3/10,1/5,1/10)\) for the minimum and \((x_{11},x_{12},x_{21},x_{30})=(1/10,1/5,1/5,1/10)\) for the maximum, filling row zero with the uniquely remaining column masses.  Each listed cell obeys \(b+w\le3\).

The common-plan identities now give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 D_{12}&=1/2-7/20=3/20,&
 D_{13}&=7/10-(7/20+7/40)=7/40,\\
 D_{21}&=7/20-1/10=1/4,&
 D_{23}&=1/5-7/40=1/40,\\
 D_{31}&=7/20+7/40-3/10=9/40,&
 D_{32}&=7/40-0=7/40,
 \end{aligned}                                             \tag{7}
\]
with zero diagonal.  Hence
\[
 (R_1,R_2,R_3)=(7/40,1/4,9/40),
 \qquad \mathcal M^\star=\{1\}.                           \tag{8}
\]
Using the separate sharp intervals (3)--(5),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 R_1^{\Box}&=\max\{0,7/10-7/20,7/10-21/40\}=7/20,\\
 R_2^{\Box}&=\max\{11/20-3/10,0,11/20-21/40\}=1/4,\\
 R_3^{\Box}&=\max\{21/40-3/10,21/40-7/20,0\}=9/40.
 \end{aligned}                                             \tag{9}
\]
The last value is uniquely smallest, so \(\mathcal M^{\Box}=\{3\}\), completing every claimed calculation.

At \(\mathsf E_3\), the three nontrivial Hall slacks, indexed by row cutoffs \(h=1,2,3\), are
\[
 \left(Q_{3-h}-\sum_{b=h}^3p_b\right)_{h=1}^3
 =(1/5,3/10,1/5).                                         \tag{1}
\]
They are strictly positive, and each is linear in \((p,q)\).

We next establish the continuity needed for a nondegenerate neighborhood.  For a fixed coefficient vector \(c=(c_b)_{b=0}^3\), let
\[
 \phi_c(p,q)=\max_{x\in\Gamma_3(p,q)}\sum_{b,w}c_bwx_{bw}. \tag{2}
\]
Fix a deterministic order for tied coefficients in the eligibility-greedy algorithm.  Its finite sequence of updates replaces a row residual and a column residual by subtracting the allocation, which is the minimum of those two nonnegative residuals.  Therefore every allocation and the resulting objective are obtained from \((p,q)\) by finitely many additions, subtractions, and minima on each eligibility pattern.  There are finitely many patterns; at a boundary the changing allocation is zero, so the adjacent objective expressions agree.  The optimal-value identity in \(\text{thm:eligibility-greedy-support}\) therefore makes \(\phi_c\) continuous and piecewise affine on the feasible-margin domain.  Moreover,
\[
 \min_{x\in\Gamma_3(p,q)}\sum_{b,w}c_bwx_{bw}=-\phi_{-c}(p,q),             \tag{3}
\]
so the corresponding minima are continuous.  The endpoint formulas use only finite sums, minima, and maxima, hence are continuous.  By the pairwise formulas in \(\text{thm:joint-value-set-and-support}\), every \(D_{mj}\) and \(D_{mj}^{\Box}\) is a continuous function of \((\pi,p,\mu,q)\); finite maximization then makes each \(R_m\) and \(R_m^{\Box}\) continuous as well.  This argument is relative to the feasible domain \(\Theta_3\) and requires neither differentiability nor a fixed active basis.

At the center point, the strict common-law-versus-box gap is
\[
 D_{12}^{\Box}-D_{12}=7/20-3/20=1/5.                     \tag{4}
\]
The shared-law regret vector and the gaps above its first coordinate are
\[
 (R_1,R_2,R_3)=(7/40,1/4,9/40),\qquad
 R_2-R_1=3/40,\quad R_3-R_1=1/20.                         \tag{5}
\]
The box regret vector and the gaps above its third coordinate are
\[
 (R_1^{\Box},R_2^{\Box},R_3^{\Box})=(7/20,1/4,9/40),\qquad
 R_1^{\Box}-R_3^{\Box}=1/8,\quad
 R_2^{\Box}-R_3^{\Box}=1/40.                             \tag{6}
\]
All finitely many quantities in (1) and (4)--(6) are positive.  Continuity therefore supplies \(\varepsilon>0\) such that every point of \(\Theta_3\) within sup-norm distance \(\varepsilon\) retains all these signs.  Shrinking \(\varepsilon\), if necessary, retains \(\pi>0\).  Equations (1), (5), and (6) then imply, respectively, strict nontrivial Hall inequalities, \(\mathcal M^\star=\{1\}\), and \(\mathcal M^{\Box}=\{3\}\); equation (4) gives \(D_{12}<D_{12}^{\Box}\).

For every nonempty \(V\subseteq\mathbb R^3\), equality with the product of its coordinate ranges would imply
\[
 \sup_{v\in V}(v_1-v_2)=\sup_{v\in V}v_1-\inf_{v\in V}v_2.               \tag{7}
\]
For \(V=\mathcal V(p_{BT},q)\), the left and right sides are \(D_{12}\) and \(D_{12}^{\Box}\).  Their strict inequality proves
\[
 \mathcal V(p_{BT},q)\subsetneq
 \prod_{m\in\mathcal M}[\underline J_m,\overline J_m].   \tag{8}
\]
Finally, the value set, its support functions, and all pairwise formulas depend on \(p_{bt}\) only through \(p_b=\sum_tp_{bt}\) and \(\mu_b=\sum_ttp_{bt}\).  Hence the same \(\varepsilon\) works for every array \(p_{bt}\) with the stipulated row sums and first-moment masses.  The resulting intersection of the sup-norm ball with \(\Theta_3\) is relatively open and contains \(\mathsf E_3\), so the separation and recommendation reversal are not knife-edge phenomena.

Let
\[
 \mathcal E_{n,\alpha}=\{((r_{bt}),(q_w))\in\mathcal I_{n,\alpha}\}.      \tag{1}
\]
By hypothesis, \(\mathsf P(\mathcal E_{n,\alpha})\ge1-\alpha\).  Work on this event.  Because the observable law is admitted by \(\mathfrak M_H\), the converse in \(\text{thm:causal-response-tree-lift}\) and \(\text{lem:triple-projection-and-extension}\) ensure \(\Gamma_H(p,q)\ne\varnothing\).  Fix any \(x\in\Gamma_H(p,q)\), and define the perspective quantities
\[
 r_{bt}=\pi p_{bt},\quad s_w=\pi q_w,\quad
 \widetilde x_{bw}=\pi x_{bw}.                            \tag{2}
\]
Landmark survival positivity gives \(\pi>0\), while probability normalization gives \(\pi=\sum_{b,t}r_{bt}\le1\).  Membership in (1) gives the cellwise constraints on \(r\), and
\[
 \underline q_w\sum_{b,t}r_{bt}\le s_w
 \le\overline q_w\sum_{b,t}r_{bt}.                       \tag{3}
\]
The transport equations and support restriction give
\[
 \sum_w\widetilde x_{bw}=\pi p_b=\sum_tr_{bt},\quad
 \sum_b\widetilde x_{bw}=\pi q_w=s_w,\quad
 \widetilde x_{bw}=0\ \text{if }b+w>H.                  \tag{4}
\]
Together with nonnegativity, (2)--(4) prove
\[
 (\mathbf r,\mathbf s,\widetilde{\mathbf x})
 \in\widehat{\mathcal P}_{n,\alpha}.                    \tag{5}
\]
The corresponding image coordinate is
\[
 \sum_{b<m,t}tr_{bt}+\sum_{b\ge m,w}w\widetilde x_{bw}
 =\pi\left(\sum_{b<m}\mu_b+\sum_{b\ge m,w}wx_{bw}\right).               \tag{6}
\]
By \(\text{thm:joint-value-set-and-support}\), (6), as \(x\) ranges over \(\Gamma_H(p,q)\), ranges over the entire causal identified set.  Since (5) holds for every such \(x\),
\[
 \mathcal V(p_{BT},q)\subseteq\widehat{\mathcal V}_{n,\alpha}
 \quad\text{on }\mathcal E_{n,\alpha}.                  \tag{7}
\]

For optimizer coverage, positivity of \(\pi\) makes scaling bijective:
\[
 \mathsf X_H(\mathbf r,\mathbf s)
 =\{\pi x:x\in\Gamma_H(p,q)\}.                           \tag{8}
\]
Substitution into the definition of \(\mathsf J_m\) yields, at the true perspective margins,
\[
 \mathsf D_{mj}(\mathbf r,\mathbf s)=D_{mj},\quad
 \mathsf R_m(\mathbf r,\mathbf s)=R_m.                   \tag{9}
\]
Those true margins lie in the projection of the confidence polytope by (5).  Thus, simultaneously for all \(m\in\mathcal M\),
\[
 \underline R_m^{n,\alpha}\le R_m\le\overline R_m^{n,\alpha}.          \tag{10}
\]
If \(m\in\mathcal M^\star\), then \(R_m=\min_jR_j\), and (10) gives
\[
 \underline R_m^{n,\alpha}\le R_m=\min_jR_j
 \le\min_j\overline R_j^{n,\alpha}.                    \tag{11}
\]
Hence \(m\in\widehat{\mathcal M}_{n,\alpha}\), proving
\[
 \mathcal M^\star\subseteq\widehat{\mathcal M}_{n,\alpha}
 \quad\text{on }\mathcal E_{n,\alpha}.                  \tag{12}
\]
No inequality in this argument is made strict, so (7) and (12) remain valid on Hall faces and retain every tied minimizer.

On the event (1), the confidence polytope is nonempty by (5).  It is closed and bounded: all coordinates are nonnegative, its total row mass is at most one, and the row and column equations bound \(s\) and \(x\) by that same total.  Hence it and its coordinate projections are compact polytopes, including candidate points of total mass zero.  The value confidence set is their linear image.  For fixed candidate margins and each \((m,j)\), \(\mathsf D_{mj}\) is the optimum of the explicitly constrained finite transport program over \(\mathsf X_H(\mathbf r,\mathbf s)\); the regret uses only a maximum over the finite menu, and the confidence envelopes optimize this finite-dimensional value over the compact projected polytope.  Thus every reported set and envelope is a finite-dimensional computable optimization object with the variables and constraints displayed in the frozen definitions.  Taking probabilities in (7) and (12) proves both claims with probability at least \(1-\alpha\).

The positive conditional assertion is set-theoretic.  For every \(\mathsf P\in\mathfrak M_H\), the proof of \(\text{thm:confidence-polytope}\) gives
\[
 \{((r_{bt}),(q_w))\in\mathcal I_{n,\alpha}\}
 \subseteq
 \{\mathcal V(p_{BT},q)\subseteq\widehat{\mathcal V}_{n,\alpha},\ 
   \mathcal M^\star\subseteq\widehat{\mathcal M}_{n,\alpha}\}.         \tag{1}
\]
Taking probabilities, then the infimum over \(\mathfrak M_H\), and finally the lower limit proves the asserted uniform outer coverage.  Because (1) uses only weak inequalities and inclusion, simultaneous Hall equalities and arbitrary policy ties require no separate regularity condition.

We next give an explicit two-law obstruction to uniformly shrinking whole-set inference.  Fix \(H\ge2\), put \(\epsilon_n=n^{-2}>0\), and construct two laws with assignment probability \(\mathsf P(R=1)=1/2\), no death, \(S_k^0=S_k^1=1\), \(B=0\), and switched residual \(W=0\).  Under law zero set the capped sustained-intensive residual \(T=0\) almost surely; under law one set \(T=H\) almost surely.  Give the standard sustained branch raw residual zero.  Observe every subject through \(k\); independently of the response tree and assignment, set \(C=K\) with probability \(\epsilon_n\) and \(C=k\) otherwise.  Thus the only nonunit censoring continuation probability is \(\epsilon_n\), which is strictly positive for every \(n\).  Independence gives the displayed arm-specific censoring-exchangeability equality, assignment is independent of the response tree, assignment and landmark survival have positive probabilities, and \(B+W=0\le H\).  The cap-fibre lift in \(\text{thm:causal-response-tree-lift}\) completes legal raw-count branches while preserving these factual paths and their observed pushforwards.  Hence both laws belong to \(\mathfrak M_H\); no uniform lower overlap bound is being smuggled into the construction.

For every \(m\in\mathcal M\subseteq\{1,\ldots,H\}\), \(B<m\) and \(\pi=1\).  The two sharp value sets are therefore the singletons
\[
 V_0=\{(0)_{m\in\mathcal M}\},\qquad
 V_1=\{(H)_{m\in\mathcal M}\}.                           \tag{2}
\]
Couple one observation under the two laws using the same assignment, censoring draw, and all histories through \(k\).  Coupled observations can differ only when \(R=1\) and \(C=K\), an event of probability \(\epsilon_n/2\le\epsilon_n\).  Coupling \(n\) independent observations coordinatewise and using the union bound gives
\[
 \left\|P_{0,n}^{\otimes n}-P_{1,n}^{\otimes n}\right\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
 \le n\epsilon_n=n^{-1}\longrightarrow0.                 \tag{3}
\]

Let \(\mathcal C_n\) be any observed-data random region with uniform asymptotic whole-value-set coverage at level \(1-\alpha\).  Applied to the two triangular sequences, uniform honesty gives
\[
 P_{0,n}^{\otimes n}(V_0\subseteq\mathcal C_n)\ge1-\alpha-o(1),\qquad
 P_{1,n}^{\otimes n}(V_1\subseteq\mathcal C_n)\ge1-\alpha-o(1).          \tag{4}
\]
Total variation in (3) transfers the second event to law zero with the same lower bound up to \(o(1)\).  A union bound under that common law then gives
\[
 P_{0,n}^{\otimes n}\{V_0\cup V_1\subseteq\mathcal C_n\}
 \ge1-2\alpha-o(1).                                      \tag{5}
\]
On this event, \(\operatorname{diam}_{\infty}(\mathcal C_n)\ge H\) by (2).  Thus there is a sequence in \(\mathfrak M_H\) along which the probability of sup-norm diameter at least \(H\) has lower limit at least \(1-2\alpha\).

For the optimizer obstruction, specialize to \(H=3\), \(\mathcal M=\{1,2,3\}\), and the common \((p,q)\) margins of \(\mathsf E_3\).  Their nontrivial Hall slacks are \((1/5,3/10,1/5)\), so legal capacity couplings exist with strict slack.  In law zero set \(T=0\) conditional on every \(B\), so \(\mu_b=0\) for all rows.  The shell extrema in \(\text{thm:eligibility-greedy-support}\) give the exact pairwise matrix
\[
 (D_{mj})_{m,j=1}^3=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 0&1/2&7/10\\
 -1/10&0&1/5\\
 -3/10&0&0
 \end{pmatrix},
\]
and hence
\[
 (R_1,R_2,R_3)=(7/10,1/5,0),\qquad \mathcal M^\star=\{3\}.               \tag{6}
\]
In law one, on row one put conditional probabilities \(5/6\) and \(1/6\) at \(T=1\) and \(T=2\), respectively; on row two put probabilities \(1/8\) and \(7/8\) at \(T=0\) and \(T=1\); and set \(T=0\) on rows zero and three.  Multiplying by the row masses gives
\[
 (\mu_0,\mu_1,\mu_2,\mu_3)=(0,7/20,7/40,0),
\]
so \(\text{prop:rational-recommendation-reversal}\) gives the unique optimizer \(\mathcal M^\star=\{1\}\).  The common \(p\) margin permits identical pre-landmark intensive histories, and the standard sustained histories and switched margins can also be identical; the response-tree lift supplies all unused branches.  Under the same censoring scheme, the two observed data laws can again differ only for a continued intensive observation, so (3) remains valid.

Let \(\mathcal K_n\subseteq\mathcal M\) be any uniformly honest outer confidence set for \(\mathcal M^\star\).  Coverage of the two unique optimizers, total-variation transfer, and the same union bound give
\[
 P_{0,n}^{\otimes n}\{\{1,3\}\subseteq\mathcal K_n\}
 \ge1-2\alpha-o(1).                                      \tag{7}
\]
Thus every uniformly honest optimizer procedure has a sequence along which both thresholds occur with limiting lower probability at least \(1-2\alpha\), even though the Hall inequalities are strict and each law has a unique optimizer.  The obstruction is vanishing information after censoring, not a Hall or policy tie.  Consequently a nonvacuous implementation of \(\mathfrak I\) must add quantitative effective assignment, survival, and censoring overlap and must control cross-fitted nuisance remainders.  The frozen assumptions contain neither uniform overlap constants nor nuisance-rate conditions, so no uniformly shrinking conclusion can be derived from them.
